The '''Einstein Institute of Mathematics''' ({{Langx|he|מָכוֹן אַייְנְשְׁטַייְן לְמָתֶמָטִיקָה}}) is a centre for [[scientific research]] in [[mathematics]] at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]], founded in 1925 with the opening of the university. A leading [[research institute]], the institute's faculty has included recipients of the [[Nobel Prize]], [[Fields Medal]], [[Wolf Prize in Mathematics|Wolf Prize]], and [[Israel Prize]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathematics.huji.ac.il/book/award-highlights|title=Award highlights|website=Einstein Institute of Mathematics|access-date=1 December 2018}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Einstein Institute Scopus Building.jpg|thumb|Historic home of the institute on [[Mount Scopus]]]]
About a year before the official inauguration of the Hebrew University, a Jewish-American philanthropist, Philip Wattenberg, endowed the new university with $190,000 (equivalent to ${{Inflation|US|.19|1925|r=1}}&nbsp;million in {{Inflation/year|US}}) for a research institute in the name of theoretical physicist [[Albert Einstein]].<ref>{{cite news |title=$190,000 Donation to Hebrew University; Philip Wattenberg of New York Gives Money for Einstein Institute |newspaper=[[New York Times]] |date=April 6, 1925 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1925/04/06/archives/190000-donation-to-hebrew-university-philip-wattenberg-of-new-york.html }}</ref><ref name=katz>{{cite journal|title=Berlin Roots – Zionist Incarnation: The Ethos of Pure Mathematics and the Beginnings of the Einstein Institute of Mathematics at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem|first=Shaul|last=Katz|journal=Science in Context|url=http://journals.cambridge.org/abstract_S0269889704000092|volume=17|issue=1–2|pages=199–234|date=2004|doi=10.1017/S0269889704000092|publisher=Cambridge University Press|s2cid=145575536 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The Einstein Mathematics-Physics Institute was established in 1925. Its [[Public lecture|inaugural lecture]] was given by [[Edmund Landau]] (on problems from [[number theory]]), the first lecture in higher mathematics to be delivered in [[modern Hebrew]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ma.huji.ac.il/~landau/landuniv.html#article|title=Edmund Landau and the Hebrew University|date=2004|website=[[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]]|access-date=1 December 2018|archive-date=3 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103030856/http://www.ma.huji.ac.il/~landau/landuniv.html#article|url-status=dead}}</ref> The Institute moved to the Philip Wattenburg Building in 1928,{{notetag|Today part of the Estelle & Eugene Ferkauf Science Teaching Centre.}} designed by Benjamin Chaikin and Sir [[Frank Mears]], where it remained until the Hebrew University lost access to [[Mount Scopus]] in 1948.

[[Edmund Landau]] served as the university's first Professor of Mathematics, and negotiated the transfer of [[Felix Klein]]'s [[private library]] from [[Göttingen]] to Jerusalem, which served as the basis for the new mathematical library in Jerusalem.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Zionist Internationalism through Number Theory: Edmund Landau at the Opening of the Hebrew University in 1925|doi=10.1017/S0269889710000177|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/science-in-context/article/zionist-internationalism-through-number-theory-edmund-landau-at-the-opening-of-the-hebrew-university-in-1925/EC6582CBB73761866BF87E0E51338CEF|first1=Leo|last1=Corry|author1-link=Leo Corry|first2=Norbert|last2=Schappacher|author2-link=Norbert Schappacher|journal=Science in Context|volume=23|issue=4|date=2010|pages=427–471|s2cid=32283386 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Other early faculty members included [[Binyamin Amirà]], [[Abraham Fraenkel]], and [[Michael Fekete]].<ref name=building>{{cite web|title=About our building|url=https://mathematics.huji.ac.il/book/about-our-building-2|website=Einstein Institute of Mathematics|access-date=1 December 2018}}</ref> A number of researchers arrived at the institute during the rise of the [[Nazi regime]] in Germany, such as [[Issai Schur]] and [[Otto Toeplitz]].{{r|katz}}

The ''[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]]'' was founded at the institute in 1963 as a continuation of the ''Bulletin of the Research Council of Israel'' (Section F).{{r|building}} A division for [[computer science]] was formed within the institute in 1969, which became the independent Institute for Computer Science in 1992.{{notetag|Now part of the Benin School of Computer Science and Engineering.}}{{r|building}}
